newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Amex launches Taiwan credit card.
newsitem.headline: Amex launches Taiwan credit card.

text.p: American Express, famous worldwide for its charge cards, launched on Tuesday a new credit card in Taiwan aimed at taking a slice of a lucrative market that has exploded under the liberalisations of recent years.
The booming Taiwan market saw some 5.5 million credit card holders use their plastic to ring up a total of T$272.4 billion (US$9.9 billion) in 1996 -- up 40 percent from 1995.

"Following an extensive market study, we decided to launch the AE credit card in Taiwan after our charge card has been issued for seven years," said Jeffrey Williams, vice president of Travel Related Services of American Express (Taiwan) Inc.
Unlike the American Express Card, which does not extend credit to holders, the AE card is a credit instrument allowing holders to pay interest if they want to stretch out payments.
Amex Taiwan marketing and sales director Susan Chen said that with rapid growth each year, the Taiwan market "definitely has great potential."
Chen said Amex has launched the credit card in only six other markets -- Hong Kong is the only one in Asia -- and was targeting not only wage-earners but also young people.

"We have noticed that the spending practices of young people here have obvious changes in recent years. They like to use credit cards, choosing to pay with revolving interest rates. And most important -- they have good credit," Chen said.
Williams said the new credit card provided the lowest revolving interest rate for card holders -- 16 percent -- compared with rates well over 20 percent for other cards.
Williams said, however, Amex would not give up the traditional American Express Card market in Taiwan, as this remained the company's core product.
American Express issued its first charge card on the island in 1987 and now has more than 200,000 members.

Ian Marsh, senior vice president and East Asian area general manager, said Amex planned to launch the credit card in Japan and other Asian nations -- even China -- but would not say which market was next.
"The vast mainland market is interesting," he said.
March said there were still a number of factors to consider in China, including tough restrictions on foreign banking and consumers' unfamiliarity with card and credit buying.
This contrasted sharply with a deeply liberalised Taiwan, which basically sets no limits on major international credit card companies issuing cards on the island.
Taiwan consumers now carry a dizzying range of major cards, including VISA, MasterCard, JCB and Diners Club.
Because of the lucrative business, which almost guarantees high profits, more than 40 institutions, including some which are not financial organisations, have issued cards in Taiwan.
Since international credit cards debuted in Taiwan in 1989, the number of card holders has rocketed by over 50 percent a year and has shown no signs of slowing.
By western standards, Taiwan's 21 million people could be expected to pack 100 million credit cards in their pockets, but statistics show only 5.5 million cards are now in circulation.
